sentences: Three reasons.

First, I've already proven myself on the front line: a year at the Hyatt front desk handling international check-ins, complaints and unexpected situations, where colleagues called me their go-to person — not for seniority, but because anything given to me never needed checking twice.
Second, I have the communication profile China Airlines needs: Mandarin, English and Korean, TOEIC 795 and TOPIK Level 4, plus actually living in Canada and Korea.
Third, I understand that in uniform I'm not representing myself — and I'm ready.

articles.title: __QUESTION_BANK__ 276
sentences: Three reasons.
First, the sensitivity to detail STARLUX asks for is exactly what I spent a year developing — noticing before a passenger speaks, like the pregnant guest whose need I picked up on.
That can't be rushed.
Second, my background matches STARLUX's passenger mix: Mandarin, English and Korean, with the Asian network weighted heavily toward Japan and Korea, so I can contribute immediately.
Third, STARLUX is still growing and needs people who execute the standard consistently and help build it.
To me that's the fit: I learn fast, I'm reliable, and I genuinely enjoy getting details right.

articles.title: __QUESTION_BANK__ 276
sentences: Three reasons.

First, my training follows the same logic as EVA's culture of discipline: I studied Public Administration and Policy and understand why systems are designed as they are, and at Hyatt I worked within standard procedures and double-checking — precisely the error-free way of working EVA expects.
Second, I have the flexibility this job needs: I've worked morning, afternoon and night shifts and lived independently in Korea from scratch.
Third, I have the service foundation and the languages.
To me the honest answer is this: I'm not the flashiest candidate, but I'll be the one who completes what she's given and stays for the long term.

articles.title: 為什麼我們航空公司一定要錄取你？
sentences: Three reasons.

First, I've already proven myself on the front line: a year at the Hyatt front desk handling international check-ins, complaints and unexpected situations, where colleagues called me their go-to person — not for seniority, but because anything given to me never needed checking twice.
Second, I have the communication profile China Airlines needs: Mandarin, English and Korean, TOEIC 795 and TOPIK Level 4, plus actually living in Canada and Korea.
Third, I understand that in uniform I'm not representing myself — and I'm ready.

articles.title: __QUESTION_BANK__ 277
sentences: I'd say consistency.
China Airlines' service spirit puts the customer first, and the interview process itself tests consistency — the second round checks whether your answers hold steady.
Mine shows up in two places.

First, service quality that doesn't fluctuate with the shift or my mood: during a year of rotating morning, afternoon and night shifts at Hyatt, the highest praise my supervisor gave me was that I maintained service quality even during the busiest periods.
Second, consistency between words and actions — everything I say is true, so however many times I'm asked or whoever asks, the answer doesn't change shape.
I also identify with how China Airlines carries Taiwanese culture to the world.
My Public Administration background trained me to think about the public value an organisation carries, and in uniform I'm not representing myself.
That awareness of representation is, I think, exactly the quality China Airlines needs.

articles.title: __QUESTION_BANK__ 277
sentences: I'd say observation — what STARLUX calls anticipation.
Its boutique positioning depends on handling things before a passenger has to ask, and that's exactly the ability I spent a year developing at Hyatt.
For example, I noticed a pregnant guest standing uncomfortably in a busy queue and checked her in first, moving her to a room near the lift.
I also picked up on a Colombian guest's hesitation with a Chinese-only interface and helped him translate his way through the online check-in.
Neither was part of my formal duties, but those are the moments guests actually remember.
The second quality I think fits is steadiness — STARLUX wants a calm kind of warmth rather than outgoing enthusiasm.
I'm not the person who works the room; my service is quiet, careful and error-free, which is the texture premium service actually needs.

articles.title: __QUESTION_BANK__ 277
sentences: I'd say discipline — or more precisely, the attitude of following first and suggesting afterwards.

EVA's corporate spirit puts flight safety in its opening line and its culture values rules and compliance, which matches my training exactly: four years of Public Administration and Policy taught me why rules are written as they are and why they aren't there to be worked around.
A concrete example from Hyatt: my supervisor once pointed out that I could have handled a guest interaction more diplomatically.
I didn't argue — I adjusted first, and only after I was performing steadily did I offer my own observation.
I believe that's the right order when it comes to rules.
A related quality is reliability: after entering the wrong room type while multitasking, I built the habit of reading each record back to confirm it, and those errors essentially disappeared.
These experiences confirmed that I work well within clear procedures and follow tasks through carefully.
I would like to bring that reliability into the cabin for the long term.

articles.title: 請用台語自我介紹（30 秒）
sentences: (Answer in Taiwanese) Hello everyone, my name is Shelly Chang.
I currently work at the Hyatt hotel front desk, serving guests from all over the world every day.
I studied in Canada and was an exchange student in Korea, and I speak Mandarin, English and Korean.
My colleagues say I'm steady — anything given to me doesn't need checking again.
I hope to bring that care and steadiness into the cabin.

articles.title: 請用台語介紹你的家鄉或一個台灣景點
sentences: (Answer in Taiwanese) I'd like to introduce Sun Moon Lake in Nantou.
The water is a deep blue-green and it's surrounded by mountains; in the early morning the mist makes it look like a painting.
You can take a boat across the lake or cycle around it — both are lovely.
Whenever foreign guests visit Taiwan I tell them they must see Sun Moon Lake at least once, because it captures Taiwan's beauty best.

articles.title: 如果遇到只講台語的長輩旅客，你會怎麼服務？
sentences: I'd speak to them in Taiwanese straight away — that's the fastest way to put them at ease.
I'd slow my pace and repeat the important things twice: the seatbelt, where the lavatory is, the meal choices.
At the hotel I met an elderly gentleman who only spoke Taiwanese, and I explained how the key card worked in Taiwanese; he kept saying how glad he was that I was there.
It taught me that for older passengers, being understood matters more than being served quickly.

articles.title: 請用台語做一段簡短的機上廣播（歡迎詞）
sentences: (Announcement in Taiwanese) Ladies and gentlemen, good day and welcome aboard our flight today.
We will be departing shortly, so please take your seat, fasten your seatbelt securely, and return your seat back and tray table to the upright position.
If there is anything you need, please let us know at any time.
We wish you a safe and comfortable journey.
Thank you.

sentences: The following practice report uses short statements to introduce a travel related topic.
This reading is intended for candidates preparing for China Airlines.
This training scenario considers how clear communication can support a comfortable cabin environment.
A passenger asks a crew member where to store a small bag before departure.
The crew member listens, checks the available space, and explains the next step in simple language.
If further assistance is required, the request is passed to an appropriate colleague.
This is a fictional communication exercise and does not replace approved safety procedures or instructions from operating crew.
The reader should make a clear distinction between a polite request, a practical explanation, and an important instruction.

The airline is preparing a practice workshop to help its teams explain service information clearly.
Staff members will compare sample announcements, discuss unfamiliar expressions, and read short messages aloud.
The workshop focuses on accurate information rather than speed.
Participants will learn to identify the main action in each sentence before adding supporting details.
A trainer will demonstrate how a calm voice and a short pause can make an important message easier to understand.
During the workshop, each participant will give a colleague time to check the message and ask questions.
The exercise also includes a discussion of respectful language when a traveler needs additional assistance at the airport.
Team members will review the same message again after receiving feedback, paying special attention to names and numbers.
An observation sheet will separate information that is clearly stated from assumptions that still require confirmation.
Rather than promising an immediate solution, staff will explain the next available step and confirm who can provide further help.
The final discussion will consider how consistent wording can support cooperation between airport colleagues and cabin crew.

sentences: The following practice report uses short statements to introduce a travel related topic.
This reading is intended for candidates preparing for EVA Air.
A visitor center is creating a short guide to a neighborhood where old buildings stand beside contemporary galleries.
Travelers can begin their walk at a public square and continue toward a quiet riverside park.
Local workshops introduce traditional craftsmanship through small exhibitions and conversations with artisans.
The guide encourages visitors to observe daily life respectfully, ask before taking photographs, and leave enough time to explore at a comfortable pace.
A nearby market offers seasonal ingredients and simple meals prepared by families who have worked there for many years.

sentences: The following practice report uses short statements to introduce a travel related topic.
This reading is intended for candidates preparing for EVA Air.
This training scenario considers how clear communication can support a comfortable cabin environment.
A passenger asks a crew member where to store a small bag before departure.
The crew member listens, checks the available space, and explains the next step in simple language.
If further assistance is required, the request is passed to an appropriate colleague.
This is a fictional communication exercise and does not replace approved safety procedures or instructions from operating crew.
The reader should make a clear distinction between a polite request, a practical explanation, and an important instruction.

A visitor center is creating a short guide to a neighborhood where old buildings stand beside contemporary galleries.
Travelers can begin their walk at a public square and continue toward a quiet riverside park.
Local workshops introduce traditional craftsmanship through small exhibitions and conversations with artisans.
The guide encourages visitors to observe daily life respectfully, ask before taking photographs, and leave enough time to explore at a comfortable pace.
A nearby market offers seasonal ingredients and simple meals prepared by families who have worked there for many years.

sentences: Although the activity is hypothetical, its description invites readers to consider how accurate information influences a traveler's experience.
This reading is intended for candidates preparing for STARLUX Airlines.
A training group is preparing a discussion about environmental responsibility in the travel industry.
Participants examine how waste reduction, careful purchasing, and clear information can support a more thoughtful visitor experience.
The exercise asks readers to distinguish a measurable result from a general statement of intention.
No environmental achievement or emissions reduction is claimed for any real airline.
Instead, the passage introduces questions that can help a reader assess a sustainability announcement more carefully.
One question concerns the period covered by a report and whether the same method was used for each comparison.
Another question asks how an organization describes the boundaries of its data and the limitations of its conclusions.
The group will discuss why a successful pilot project does not automatically demonstrate the same result across an entire network.
Readers are encouraged to recognize terms such as environmental, operational, and initiatives without treating unfamiliar language as evidence of progress.
The facilitator will invite participants to propose a practical question that could clarify an incomplete public statement.
The discussion emphasizes transparency and evidence while acknowledging that improvements may involve several teams and different time frames.

articles.title: lab-2-7-0-0 · A More Understandable Terminal · 初級
articles.source: Fly Room 原創訓練稿；非官方新聞、非官方面試題
sentences: The following practice report uses short statements to introduce a travel related topic.
This reading is intended for candidates preparing for STARLUX Airlines.
A fictional airport team is reviewing signs and passenger information inside a terminal.
The project focuses on helping travelers locate transfer desks, waiting areas, and accessible facilities.
Staff will test whether a person can understand a sign without already knowing the building.
The team will also compare written directions with information provided at a service counter.
This is a simulated industry briefing and does not announce construction, a terminal opening, or a service change at a real airport.
